assessment.rationale: This is a poor direct fit for the scenario: the simulation tests filename/path-suffix type binding in CAS, not ring forwarding or per-hop authorization behavior. It is still useful negative evidence because any hop that authorizes based on path-local suffixes can make inconsistent decisions about the same CID bytes after rename, relay, or archival movement.
strengths: Negative-control purpose is explicit and easy to audit.
Failure is concrete: identical CID bytes can be reinterpreted under different suffixes.
Small specimen clearly exposes why local path names are not portable protocol evidence.
weaknesses: Does not model ring breakage, hop skipping, refusal recording, or membership reconfiguration.
Conflates local storage naming with portable CAS object semantics.
Provides no promise-first authorization or refusal artifact vocabulary.
risks: Per-hop authorization may vary by filename instead of content, causing inconsistent forward/refuse outcomes across peers.
Renames, gateways, or archive layout changes can silently alter apparent type semantics.
Audit trails become non-durable because path-local labels are not stable cross-peer evidence.
open_questions: Could suffixes be kept only as local hints while authorization binds strictly to bytes plus explicit protocol identifiers?
What portable refusal record would a real transport design need so per-hop authorization failure stays auditable across peers?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.
